name: The Melian obsidian trade

claims.text: Melian obsidian reached the Greek mainland by c. 11,000 BC.
Obsidian can be chemically traced to its source volcano.
Its presence at Franchthi Cave demonstrates open-water voyaging.

summary: Volcanic glass from the island of Melos was shipped across the Aegean from the Mesolithic onwards — the earliest evidence of seafaring in the region.
body:
Obsidian from Melos was found in the Franchthi Cave in the Argolid in layers dating to around 11,000 BC. Melos is an island and was never connected to the mainland, so someone crossed open water to get it — the earliest hard evidence for sea travel anywhere in the Mediterranean.

Obsidian gives a cutting edge sharper than surgical steel and can be chemically fingerprinted to its source volcano, so its distribution maps ancient exchange with unusual precision. A distribution map cannot tell us whether specialist sailors, direct visitors or repeated hand-to-hand exchanges carried each piece. Melian obsidian nevertheless turns up across the Aegean for eight thousand years.

name: Height of Cycladic figurine production

claims.text: Cycladic figurines were carved from marble using abrasives rather than metal tools.
They were originally painted, with traces still detectable.
Most were made for funerary deposition.
Extensive looting has destroyed the context of most known examples.
They represent a mother goddess.

summary: The distinctive folded-arm marble figurines of the Cyclades were produced in quantity for burial.
body:
Carved from local white marble with abrasives — no metal tools were needed — the figurines range from a few centimetres to nearly life size. They were painted: traces of blue and red survive, and "ghosts" of weathered paint show eyes, hair and facial markings on faces we now perceive as blank.

Most cannot stand; the feet point downwards, so they were made to lie down, consistent with burial. Their spare geometry influenced Brancusi, Modigliani and Moore.

Their popularity created a serious problem. Looting to supply the twentieth-century art market destroyed the archaeological context of the great majority, so most known figurines cannot be securely dated or interpreted.

name: Destruction of the House of the Tiles

claims.text: The House of the Tiles was destroyed by fire around 2200 BC.
Numerous Early Helladic II sites were disrupted in the same broad period.
A severe aridification event affected the Near East around 2200 BC.
The destructions were caused by invading Greek speakers.

summary: The monumental administrative building at Lerna burned around 2200 BC, part of a wider disruption across mainland Greece.
body:
The fire that ended the House of the Tiles is one node in a pattern: many Early Helladic II settlements in the Argolid and beyond were destroyed or abandoned within a few generations around 2200 BC.

Explanations have cycled through invasion by incoming Indo-European speakers, internal conflict, and — currently most favoured — the 4.2 kiloyear climate event, a severe aridification episode documented across the Near East and implicated in the collapse of the Akkadian Empire and Egypt's Old Kingdom at almost the same time.

The fire preserved hundreds of clay sealings, so the destruction is also the reason we know how the building worked.

name: The first Minoan palaces

claims.text: Palatial complexes appear on Crete from c. 1900 BC.
They combined storage, craft production, administration and ritual functions.
Administrative record-keeping using written scripts accompanied their emergence.
The first palaces were destroyed c. 1700 BC by earthquake.

summary: Around 1900 BC large multi-functional complexes appear at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros — the first states in Europe.
body:
The First Palace period marks a step change: centralised storage on an industrial scale, craft workshops, and administration recorded in Cretan Hieroglyphic and then Linear A. Storage capacity at Knossos alone ran to hundreds of thousands of litres.

Why this happened on Crete and not the mainland is debated. Crete escaped the destructions of c. 2200 BC, sits at the crossing point of Egyptian, Levantine and Aegean routes, and produced surplus oil and wine that reward central storage and redistribution.

All the first palaces were destroyed around 1700 BC, probably by earthquake, and immediately rebuilt on a grander scale.

name: The Theran eruption

claims.text: The Theran eruption was among the largest volcanic events of the Holocene.
Tsunami deposits associated with the eruption have been identified on Crete.
Radiocarbon and ice-core evidence support a date of c. 1620–1600 BC.
Egyptian archaeological synchronisms support a later date of c. 1500 BC.
The eruption directly caused the collapse of Minoan civilisation.
The eruption inspired Plato's account of Atlantis.

summary: One of the largest volcanic eruptions of the last ten thousand years destroyed the island of Thera and buried the town of Akrotiri.
body:
The eruption ejected an estimated 60 cubic kilometres of material, collapsing the centre of the island into a caldera 12 km across. Ash fell across the eastern Mediterranean and has been identified in cores from the Nile delta to the Black Sea, making it a chronological marker for the whole region.

Tsunamis struck northern Crete; deposits containing marine shells, pottery and animal bone have been found inland at Palaikastro.

The date is a long-running dispute. Radiocarbon dating of an olive branch buried alive in the ash and Greenland ice-core acidity spikes support c. 1620–1600 BC. Egyptian synchronisms from pottery cross-dating suggest c. 1500 BC. A century separates the two, which matters enormously: the high chronology means the eruption cannot have caused the Cretan destructions of 1450 BC.

name: The Mycenae shaft graves

claims.text: The Mycenae shaft graves date to c. 1650–1500 BC and contained exceptional gold assemblages.
Grave goods include Baltic amber and Egyptian-influenced imagery.
The burials predate the traditional date of the Trojan War by roughly three centuries.
The wealth derives from Mycenaean mercenary service abroad.

summary: Six deep shaft graves at Mycenae, used c. 1650–1500 BC, held the richest burials yet found in Bronze Age Europe.
body:
Grave Circle A held nineteen bodies with around 15 kg of gold: five funerary masks, gold breastplates, diadems, hundreds of gold discs sewn onto clothing, bronze daggers inlaid with gold and silver hunting scenes, amber from the Baltic, and ostrich eggs from Africa.

The wealth is a puzzle. It appears suddenly, in a society with no preceding tradition of such display. Proposals include Mycenaean mercenaries returning enriched from Egyptian service — the daggers show Nilotic scenes — and control of trade routes.

Schliemann found them in 1876 and identified them with Agamemnon's household. They are roughly three centuries too early. He was wrong about the identification and right that something remarkable was buried there.

name: The Cretan destructions of c. 1450 BC

claims.text: Most Minoan centres outside Knossos were destroyed or abandoned c. 1450 BC.
Knossos continued in use with Linear B administration in Greek.
Warrior burials with mainland weapon types appear on Crete in this phase.
The destructions resulted from Mycenaean conquest.

summary: Almost every Minoan centre on Crete was destroyed within a short period; only Knossos continued, thereafter administered in Greek.
body:
Zakros, Phaistos, Malia, Gournia and Ayia Triada were all destroyed or abandoned around 1450 BC, many with evidence of burning. Knossos survived and its administration continued — now writing Linear B, in Greek.

The simplest reading is Mycenaean conquest: a mainland takeover of the island, with Knossos retained as the administrative centre. Supporting evidence includes warrior burials with mainland-style weapons appearing on Crete and the shift in script and language.

The eruption of Thera is too early on the high chronology to be the direct cause, though longer-term economic damage may have weakened Crete beforehand.

name: Linear B administration at Knossos

claims.text: Linear B was used at Knossos for palace administration after c. 1450 BC.
Linear B records an early form of Greek.
The tablets survive because fire baked the unfired clay.
The tablets name deities later worshipped in Classical Greece.

summary: After c. 1450 BC the Knossos archives are kept in Linear B — an adaptation of Minoan Linear A used to write Greek.
body:
The tablets record flocks, textile production, chariot components, land, workers, and offerings to gods including Poseidon and a "Mistress of the Labyrinth". They are administrative records covering roughly a single cycle, not literature or a royal chronicle. Unfired clay was a temporary medium; the archive survived only because destruction fire accidentally baked it hard.

That the language is Greek is decisive: Greek-speakers were administering Crete from Knossos after the destruction of most other Cretan palace centres. Linear B was adapted from Linear A and fits Greek awkwardly, omitting final consonants and collapsing several sounds into the same signs. Its decipherment pushed the attested history of Greek back some five centuries beyond Homer while exposing the economic routines behind palace power.

name: The Trojan War (traditional)

claims.text: Greek tradition dated the Trojan War to the late 13th or early 12th century BC.
Troy VIIa was destroyed by fire around 1180 BC.
Hittite texts record a place Wilusa and a power called Ahhiyawa.
A Mycenaean Greek conflict at Troy occurred in some form.
The Iliad preserves an accurate account of a historical campaign.
Helen, Achilles and Agamemnon were historical individuals.

summary: The ten-year siege of Troy by a Greek coalition under Agamemnon — the central event of Greek legend, and possibly of Greek memory.
body:
Greek tradition placed the war firmly in history. Eratosthenes dated it to 1194–1184 BC, and Greeks reckoned their heroic past from it.

The evidence divides. Troy VIIa was destroyed by fire around 1180 BC with arrowheads and unburied bodies in the ruins. Hittite archives name a city Wilusa in the region, a king Alaksandu (compare Alexandros, Paris' other name), and repeated friction with Ahhiyawa — a power across the sea generally identified as Mycenaean. A conflict at this place involving Greeks is entirely plausible.

What the evidence does not support is the *Iliad*'s war: a thousand ships, a ten-year siege, a coalition of named kings. The poems reached their form four centuries later, and their world is a composite. The honest position is that something happened at Troy, and the Iliad is not a report of it.

name: Destruction of the Mycenaean palaces

claims.text: All major Mycenaean palace centres were destroyed or abandoned c. 1200–1180 BC.
Linear B literacy ceased with the palace system.
Late defensive works indicate the palaces anticipated a threat.
A single cause explains the destructions.
A Dorian invasion caused the collapse.

summary: Every major Mycenaean palace was destroyed or abandoned within a generation, ending palatial civilisation in Greece.
body:
Pylos burned. Mycenae and Tiryns were damaged and their citadels contracted. Thebes was destroyed. Within perhaps thirty years the entire palace system was gone, and with it Linear B literacy, monumental construction, fresco painting, and the administrative apparatus that organised production.

No single cause is agreed. Candidates include drought documented in pollen cores, earthquake sequences, internal revolt, disruption of tin supply, and raiding. The late investment in fortifications and secure water supplies at three separate citadels indicates the threat was anticipated.

Some settlements continued at a reduced scale, and pottery styles evolve continuously — this was systems failure rather than depopulation. But nobody built a palace in Greece again for six hundred years.

name: The Sea Peoples

claims.text: Egyptian inscriptions name multiple groups attacking in coalition c. 1177 BC.
Reliefs depict them moving with families and possessions.
"Sea Peoples" is a modern term, not an ancient collective name.
They were a symptom of the collapse as much as a cause.
They constituted a single unified nation or invasion.

summary: Coalitions of displaced peoples attacked Egypt and the Levant by land and sea during the Bronze Age Collapse.
body:
Egyptian inscriptions under Merneptah and Ramesses III name groups — Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen, Weshesh, Sherden — attacking in combination. The Medinet Habu reliefs show them travelling with families in ox-carts, which reads as migration rather than a raid.

Ramesses III's text says these groups had already destroyed Hatti, Carchemish, Arzawa and Alashiya — matching the archaeological destruction horizon closely.

The term "Sea Peoples" is a modern coinage; no ancient source uses it as a collective name. Current thinking treats them less as a cause of the collapse than as a symptom: populations set in motion by drought and state failure, who then accelerated the failure elsewhere.

name: Fall of Hattusa

claims.text: Hattusa was destroyed by fire and abandoned around 1190 BC.
Archives and valuables appear to have been removed before the destruction.
Late Hittite texts record grain shortages and emergency imports.

summary: The Hittite capital was burned and abandoned around 1190 BC, ending one of the great powers of the Late Bronze Age.
body:
Hattusa in central Anatolia had been the seat of an empire that fought Egypt to a draw at Kadesh. Around 1190 BC it burned and was abandoned.

Excavation suggests the collapse was not simply violent: the royal archives and treasuries appear to have been emptied before the fire, and parts of the city were already being abandoned. This looks like a state coming apart, then a final destruction.

The Hittite archives include letters recording grain shortages and appeals for emergency shipments in the empire's last decades — direct testimony to the food crisis behind the wider collapse.

name: Destruction of Ugarit

claims.text: Ugarit was destroyed around 1185 BC and never reoccupied.
Final letters record enemy ships and absent defensive forces.
Ugaritic scribes used an early cuneiform alphabetic script.

summary: The Syrian port of Ugarit was destroyed around 1185 BC, its final letters still in the kiln.
body:
Ugarit was a wealthy cosmopolitan port whose archives are written in at least eight languages, and whose scribes developed a cuneiform alphabet of thirty signs.

The last letters found there are extraordinary. The king writes that enemy ships have appeared, that his own fleet is away in Lycia and his troops in Hatti, and that the country is undefended. Another asks the king of Alashiya for help. Some were found still in the kiln where they were being baked, never sent.

The city was destroyed and never reoccupied. The tablets were preserved by the fire that ended it.

name: The Ionian migration

claims.text: Greek settlement expanded along the western Anatolian coast from c. 1050 BC.
Dialect distribution in Anatolia matches the traditional migration pattern.
Ionia became the leading centre of early Greek intellectual activity.
The migration was organised and led from Athens as tradition claims.

summary: Greek-speaking populations settled the western coast of Anatolia, founding the cities of Ionia.
body:
Greek tradition held that refugees from the mainland, led from Athens, settled the Anatolian coast after the collapse. Archaeology confirms Greek material culture appearing at Miletus, Ephesus, Colophon and elsewhere from around 1050 BC — though at Miletus there had already been Mycenaean presence.

The dialect map supports the tradition: Ionic in the centre, Aeolic to the north, Doric to the south, matching the claimed origins of the settlers.

Ionia became the most economically and intellectually dynamic part of the Greek world. Homer, Thales, Anaximander, Heraclitus, Hecataeus and Herodotus all came from this coast.

name: The Lefkandi hero burial

claims.text: The Lefkandi Toumba building dates to c. 1000–950 BC.
It covered a double burial with four sacrificed horses.
Grave goods included Near Eastern and Cypriot imports.
The find substantially revised the "Dark Age" model.

summary: A monumental building erected over a rich double burial with four sacrificed horses, around 1000 BC.
body:
The Toumba building at Lefkandi was 50 m long with an external colonnade — three centuries before any comparable Greek structure — and was deliberately demolished and buried under a mound soon after construction.

Beneath it: a cremated man in a Cypriot bronze amphora with an iron sword; an inhumed woman with gold hair-coils, a gold pectoral and a Babylonian pendant already 700 years old when buried; and a shaft with four horses.

The find dismantled the assumption that the Dark Age was uniformly poor and disconnected. Elite wealth, monumental building, heroic burial ritual and long-distance imports were all present at the supposed low point.

name: Adoption of the Greek alphabet

claims.text: The Greek alphabet derives from a Phoenician consonantal script.
Greeks repurposed unused Phoenician consonant signs as vowel letters.
The earliest Greek alphabetic inscriptions date to c. 750–740 BC.
The earliest known inscriptions are informal rather than administrative.
The alphabet was adopted specifically to record Homeric epic.

summary: Greeks adapted the Phoenician consonantal script and repurposed unused signs as vowels — creating the first full alphabet.
body:
Phoenician script wrote consonants only, which works for Semitic languages built on consonantal roots. Greek needs vowels: without them, common words become ambiguous.

The Greek solution was elegant. Phoenician had consonants Greek did not use — the glottal stop *aleph*, the pharyngeal *ayin*, *he*, *yod*. Greeks took those signs and assigned them to vowels: alpha, omicron, epsilon, iota. One notational change made the script able to represent any word in the language unambiguously, and made literacy learnable in weeks rather than years.

The earliest inscriptions — the Dipylon oinochoe from Athens and "Nestor's Cup" from Pithekoussai, both around 740 BC — are not administrative. One is a dancing prize and the other a joke about a drinking cup, written in verse. Greek writing enters the record as play.

name: The first Olympiad

claims.text: Greek chronology was reckoned in four-year Olympiads from a traditional start of 776 BC.
Votive dedications at Olympia increase markedly in the 8th century BC.
The Games continued for more than a millennium.
Games were actually first held in 776 BC.

summary: The traditional date of the first Olympic Games, which became the anchor of Greek chronology.
body:
Greek historians dated events by counting four-year Olympiads from 776 BC, the year the runner Koroibos of Elis was said to have won the *stadion*. It gave the Greek world its first shared chronological framework — essential for a civilisation of hundreds of independent states with their own calendars and magistrate-year dating.

Archaeology at Olympia shows dedications increasing sharply in the eighth century, consistent with a festival growing in importance around then, though it cannot confirm a specific year.

The Games ran for over a thousand years until Theodosius I suppressed pagan festivals around AD 393.

name: Greek colonisation of the Mediterranean

claims.text: Greeks founded settlements across the Mediterranean and Black Sea c. 750–550 BC.
Colonies were politically independent of their mother cities.
Delphi was routinely consulted before colonial foundations.
The Latin alphabet descends from Greek script transmitted via Etruria.
Land shortage was the principal driver of colonisation.

summary: Between roughly 750 and 550 BC Greeks founded hundreds of settlements from Spain to the Black Sea.
body:
Colonies were founded by a mother city, led by an appointed *oikistes*, usually after consulting Delphi — which accumulated remarkable geographic knowledge as a result. The new city was politically independent from the start, keeping cultic and sentimental ties but not obedience.

Drivers included land shortage, political conflict at home, and trade. Chalcis and Eretria settled Sicily and Italy; Miletus dominated the Black Sea; Phocaea reached Massalia and Spain; Corinth founded Syracuse and Corcyra.

The consequences were enormous: the Greek language and alphabet spread around the Mediterranean, the alphabet reached the Etruscans and through them the Romans, and the wine grape and olive were carried to France and Italy.

name: The invention of coinage

claims.text: The earliest standardised stamped coinage was produced in Lydia in the late 7th century BC.
The first coins were struck in electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy.
Croesus introduced separate gold and silver coinages.
Athenian silver coinage circulated widely beyond Athenian territory.

summary: Lydia produced the first standardised stamped coins in electrum in the late seventh century BC; Greek cities adopted the idea within a generation.
body:
The first coins were lumps of electrum — a natural gold-silver alloy from the Pactolus river — of controlled weight, stamped with a design guaranteeing them. The stamp converts metal into money by removing the need to weigh and assay at every transaction.

Croesus later separated the alloy into pure gold and silver coinages, creating the first bimetallic system with a fixed exchange rate.

Greek cities adopted coinage rapidly and made it identity: the Athenian owl, the Aeginetan turtle, the Corinthian pegasus. Athens' silver owls, backed by Laurion, became the first international reserve currency, accepted from Egypt to the Black Sea. Coin hoards are now among the most precise dating tools in archaeology.

name: The reforms of Solon

claims.text: Solon cancelled debts and prohibited loans secured on the person.
He created four property-based classes determining eligibility for office.
He extended jury participation and the right to prosecute on another's behalf.
He redistributed land.

summary: Solon cancelled debts, abolished debt-slavery and opened office by wealth rather than birth, defusing a crisis at Athens.
body:
Athens in 594 BC faced revolt: farmers were falling into debt-bondage and being sold abroad. Solon was given extraordinary powers to legislate.

The *seisachtheia* cancelled existing debts, freed those enslaved for them, and outlawed loans secured on the person. He then replaced birth with income as the qualification for office, creating four property classes, and gave even the poorest citizens the right to sit on juries and to prosecute on behalf of a wronged party — the first general right of legal action.

He left Athens for a decade so he could not be pressured to change the laws. He satisfied nobody fully, and said so in his own poetry.

name: The Peisistratid tyranny

claims.text: Peisistratus and his sons controlled Athens from 561 to 510 BC with interruptions.
Hipparchus was assassinated in 514 BC by Harmodius and Aristogeiton.
Hippias was expelled from Athens in 510 BC with Spartan assistance.
The tyrannicides acted for political rather than personal motives.

summary: Peisistratus and his sons ruled Athens for half a century, expanding festivals and public works before being expelled.
body:
Peisistratus took power three times, ruling securely from 546 BC. His regime was not straightforwardly repressive: he kept Solon's laws, sent judges into the countryside to reduce dependence on local aristocrats, funded public works and water supply, expanded the Panathenaia, and gave the City Dionysia its dramatic competitions.

His sons Hippias and Hipparchus succeeded him. Hipparchus was assassinated in 514 BC by Harmodius and Aristogeiton — over a personal quarrel, though Athens later remembered them as democratic martyrs and put up the first political statues in Greek history. Hippias grew harsh and was expelled in 510 BC with Spartan help. He later guided the Persians to Marathon.

name: The reforms of Cleisthenes

claims.text: Cleisthenes created ten tribes composed of trittyes from three separate regions.
The Council of 500 was selected by lot, fifty from each tribe.
Citizens were registered through their deme.
The reforms were designed to break regional aristocratic power.

summary: Athens was reorganised into ten artificial tribes drawn from across Attica, creating the structure of democracy.
body:
Cleisthenes divided Attica into three regions — city, coast, inland — split each into ten *trittyes*, and built each new tribe from one trittys of each region. A tribe therefore had no geographical coherence and no aristocratic patron, which destroyed the regional power bases that had driven a century of factional conflict.

Citizenship was registered by *deme*, the local ward, and the demotic replaced patronymic in official contexts. The Council of 500 — fifty from each tribe by lot — prepared assembly business, and its presiding committee rotated ten times a year.

The result was a system in which most citizens would hold office at some point, and in which the machinery itself resisted capture by any family.

name: The Ionian Revolt

claims.text: Ionian Greek cities revolted against Persian rule from 499 to 493 BC.
Athens and Eretria sent naval support to the rebels.
Sardis was burned during the revolt.
Persia destroyed Miletus in 494 BC.

summary: The Greek cities of Asia Minor rebelled against Persian rule; Athens sent help, and Persia did not forget it.
body:
Aristagoras of Miletus provoked the revolt in 499 BC. Athens and Eretria sent twenty-five ships; the rebels marched inland and burned Sardis, the Persian regional capital. Herodotus reports Darius asking who the Athenians were, and instructing a servant to repeat "Master, remember the Athenians" at every dinner.

Persia crushed the revolt at the naval battle of Lade in 494 and destroyed Miletus, killing or deporting its population.

The consequences were out of proportion to the ships involved: Athenian participation gave Darius his justification for the expedition that ended at Marathon, and so for the whole Persian Wars.

name: Battle of Marathon
outcome: Decisive Greek victory

claims.text: Athenian and Plataean forces defeated a Persian army at Marathon in 490 BC.
The Greek centre was deliberately thinned to extend the line.
The Athenian dead were buried in a mound on the battlefield.
Herodotus' casualty figures are accurate.

summary: Athenian and Plataean hoplites defeated a larger Persian landing force in 490 BC — the first Greek victory over Persia.
body:
The Persians landed at Marathon intending to draw the Athenian army out and take the city. Athens marched to meet them with about 10,000 hoplites and 1,000 Plataeans against a Persian force of perhaps 25,000.

Miltiades thinned the Greek centre to extend the line and avoid being outflanked, and strengthened the wings. The Greeks advanced at a run over the last stretch to minimise time under archery. The centre gave ground as expected; the wings won and turned inward, enveloping the Persian centre.

Herodotus gives 6,400 Persian dead against 192 Athenians. The Athenians then marched roughly 40 km back to Athens the same day to face the Persian fleet, which sailed away.

The result mattered beyond the numbers: Persian infantry, in the open, could be beaten by hoplites.

name: Battle of Thermopylae
outcome: Persian victory; Greek rearguard annihilated

claims.text: A Greek force held the pass at Thermopylae for three days in 480 BC.
The position was turned by a mountain path revealed to the Persians.
Persian arrowheads excavated on Kolonos hill confirm the final stand.
Around 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans remained at the end.
Xerxes' army numbered in the millions.

summary: A Greek force under Leonidas held the pass for three days against Xerxes' army before being outflanked and destroyed.
body:
Around 7,000 Greeks blocked a pass a few metres wide, where Persian numbers counted for nothing. For two days assaults failed, including attacks by the elite Immortals.

A local man, Ephialtes, showed the Persians the Anopaia path over the mountain. Learning he was surrounded, Leonidas dismissed most of the army and stayed with 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans. The Thespians' choice to stay is often forgotten and was entirely voluntary.

They were pushed back to a hillock and killed by missiles — confirmed by the Persian arrowheads Marinatos excavated there. The delay let the Greek fleet withdraw in order and gave the southern states time to prepare.

name: Battle of Salamis
outcome: Decisive Greek naval victory

claims.text: The Greek fleet defeated a larger Persian fleet at Salamis in 480 BC.
The battle was fought in narrow straits that negated Persian numbers.
Themistocles used deception to bring on the engagement.
Aeschylus was present at the battle.

summary: The Greek fleet destroyed a much larger Persian navy in the narrows off Salamis, breaking the invasion.
body:
With Athens evacuated and burning, the Greek fleet of around 370 ships faced perhaps 600–800 Persian vessels. The allies wanted to withdraw to the Isthmus; Themistocles argued for fighting in the straits, and reportedly forced the issue by sending a servant to Xerxes claiming the Greeks were about to flee.

Xerxes blocked both exits and waited, then watched from a throne on the shore. In the narrows the Persian fleet could not use its numbers; ships fouled each other, and the heavier Greek triremes rammed into the confusion.

Aeschylus fought in the battle and staged it eight years later in *The Persians*, from the perspective of the Persian court — the only surviving Greek tragedy on a contemporary event, written by a participant.

name: Battle of Plataea
outcome: Decisive Greek victory; Persian land forces destroyed

claims.text: A Greek coalition destroyed the Persian land army at Plataea in 479 BC.
Mardonius was killed in the battle.
It was among the largest hoplite engagements recorded.
The Greek victory at Mycale occurred at nearly the same time.

summary: The largest hoplite battle ever fought ended the Persian invasion of Greece in 479 BC.
body:
Some 40,000 Greek hoplites under the Spartan regent Pausanias faced Mardonius' army left behind after Salamis. After days of manoeuvring over water supplies, a confused Greek night withdrawal left the line dispersed, and Mardonius attacked what he took for a rout.

The Spartans and Tegeans held under sustained archery, then closed. In hand-to-hand fighting the Persian infantry, without comparable armour or the long spear, was broken. Mardonius was killed and the army collapsed.

On the same days the Greeks destroyed the Persian fleet's base at Mycale. The invasion was over, and the initiative passed to the Greeks — which is where the Delian League, and Athenian empire, begin.

name: The Delian League

claims.text: The Delian League was founded in 478/7 BC with its treasury on Delos.
The treasury was moved to Athens in 454 BC.
Athenian Tribute Lists record annual payments by member states.
Athens used force to prevent members from leaving.
League funds were used for the Acropolis building programme.

summary: An alliance against Persia founded in 478 BC that Athens converted within a generation into an empire.
body:
Members contributed ships or cash to a common treasury on Delos, with Athens providing leadership. The alliance succeeded: Persia was pushed out of the Aegean.

It then became something else. States that tried to leave were besieged and forced back — Naxos in 470, Thasos in 465. Most members found it easier to pay cash than provide ships, which meant Athens built the ships and had the fleet. In 454 the treasury was moved to Athens, and tribute began funding the Parthenon. Athenian coinage, weights and measures were imposed; major legal cases were transferred to Athenian courts.

The Athenian Tribute Lists — inscribed records of the one-sixtieth of each payment dedicated to Athena — survive on stone, giving a year-by-year account of who paid what.

name: Construction of the Parthenon

claims.text: The Parthenon was built between 447 and 432 BC.
Its horizontal lines curve and its columns incline inward.
A Venetian bombardment detonated an Ottoman powder store inside in 1687.
Roughly half the surviving sculpture was removed by Lord Elgin.
The architectural refinements were intended as optical corrections.

summary: The temple of Athena Parthenos was built on the Acropolis in fifteen years, funded substantially by imperial tribute.
body:
Iktinos and Kallikrates were the architects, Pheidias directed the sculpture. Some 22,000 tonnes of Pentelic marble were quarried 16 km away and hauled up the Acropolis.

Almost nothing in it is straight. The stylobate curves upward about 11 cm at the centre; columns lean inward and would meet roughly 2.4 km above; corner columns are slightly thicker; each has a subtle *entasis* bulge. These refinements were cut into individual blocks with no possibility of adjustment afterwards, and the standard explanation — optical correction — is plausible but not proven.

The building has served as temple, church, mosque and gunpowder store. In 1687 a Venetian shell detonated the Ottoman magazine inside and blew out the centre. Lord Elgin removed roughly half the surviving sculpture between 1801 and 1812; the question of its return remains open.

name: The Peloponnesian War
outcome: Spartan victory; Athenian empire dissolved

claims.text: Athens and Sparta fought from 431 to 404 BC, ending in Athenian defeat.
Plague struck Athens in 430 BC, killing a large proportion of the population.
Persian subsidies funded the Spartan fleet in the final phase.
Athens surrendered after the loss of its fleet at Aegospotami.
Thucydides' analysis of the war's cause is broadly correct.

summary: Twenty-seven years of war between Athens and Sparta that exhausted Greece and ended the Athenian empire.
body:
Thucydides identified the underlying cause plainly: the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta.

The first decade set a land power against a sea power with no way for either to reach the other decisively. Pericles brought Attica's population inside the walls and relied on the fleet — sound strategy ruined when plague broke out in the crowded city in 430 BC and killed perhaps a quarter of the population, including Pericles.

The Sicilian Expedition of 415–413 BC destroyed an entire Athenian army and fleet. Sparta then took Persian money, built a fleet, and under Lysander destroyed the Athenian navy at Aegospotami in 405. Athens, cut off from Black Sea grain, surrendered in 404.

Both sides were exhausted, and Persia — which had funded the winner — recovered the Greek cities of Asia within a decade.

name: The Plague of Athens

claims.text: An epidemic struck Athens from 430 BC and recurred through 426 BC.
Thucydides contracted the disease and recorded its symptoms in detail.
Pericles died of the disease in 429 BC.
A mass burial of the period has been excavated in the Kerameikos.
The disease was typhoid fever.

summary: An epidemic in the overcrowded wartime city killed perhaps a quarter of the Athenian population, including Pericles.
body:
Thucydides caught the disease, survived, and described it clinically — fever, inflamed eyes, bleeding from mouth and throat, pustules, unquenchable thirst, and death typically on the seventh or eighth day. He wrote the description explicitly so it could be recognised if it returned, which is a scientific motive.

He also recorded the social effects: people died untended because carers caught it, corpses lay in temples, funeral rites were abandoned, and lawlessness spread as people saw no reason to restrain themselves for a future they might not have.

Proposed identifications include typhus, typhoid, smallpox, measles and viral haemorrhagic fever. DNA from a Kerameikos mass grave in 2006 suggested typhoid, but the analysis has been contested on contamination grounds. It remains unresolved.

name: The Sicilian Expedition

claims.text: Athens launched an expedition against Syracuse in 415 BC that was destroyed by 413 BC.
Alcibiades promoted the expedition and defected after being recalled.
The Athenian fleet was destroyed in the Great Harbour of Syracuse.
Surviving prisoners were held in the stone quarries.

summary: Athens sent its largest ever expedition against Syracuse; it was annihilated, and the empire never recovered.
body:
Alcibiades persuaded the assembly to attack Syracuse — a city as large as Athens, on the far side of the Mediterranean, while at war with Sparta. Nicias opposed it, then tried to deter the assembly by describing the enormous force required. They voted him the enormous force and put him in command of an operation he thought was a mistake.

Alcibiades was recalled for trial almost immediately and defected. The siege stalled; Sparta sent a commander who broke it. Reinforcements arrived and failed too.

When the fleet was destroyed in the Great Harbour, the survivors retreated overland and were cut down or captured. Around 40,000 men were lost. Prisoners were held in the stone quarries; Plutarch says some earned better treatment by reciting Euripides, whose poetry the Syracusans admired.

name: Battle of Aegospotami
outcome: Decisive Spartan victory

claims.text: Lysander captured the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BC.
The Athenian ships were taken while beached and largely unmanned.
The defeat cut Athens off from Black Sea grain and forced surrender.
Alcibiades warned the Athenian commanders beforehand.

summary: Lysander destroyed the Athenian fleet on the beach in 405 BC, ending the Peloponnesian War within months.
body:
The Athenian fleet was beached on an open shore in the Hellespont with no proper base, and its crews dispersed daily to find food. Lysander watched this for four days. On the fifth he attacked while the ships were empty and captured almost the entire fleet — around 170 ships — with barely a fight.

Alcibiades, living nearby in exile, had ridden down to warn the Athenian commanders that their position was indefensible. They told him to go away.

With the fleet gone, the Black Sea grain route was cut. Athens was starved out and surrendered in 404 BC.

name: The trial of Socrates

claims.text: Socrates was tried in 399 BC on charges of impiety and corrupting the young.
He was convicted and executed by hemlock.
He declined an opportunity to escape.
The prosecution was politically motivated.
Plato's Apology reports the actual defence speech.

summary: Socrates was tried before 500 Athenian jurors for impiety and corrupting the young, convicted, and executed.
body:
The charges were introducing new gods and corrupting the youth. The political background is unavoidable: Athens had lost the war, suffered the Thirty Tyrants, and several of Socrates' associates — Critias, Charmides, Alcibiades — had been prominent in the oligarchy or its betrayals. An amnesty barred prosecuting them for it, but not this.

Plato's *Apology* has Socrates refuse to plead for mercy, compare himself to a gadfly stinging a sluggish horse, and propose free meals at public expense as his counter-penalty. He was convicted by around 280 to 220; more jurors voted for death than for conviction, suggesting the counter-proposal cost him.

He declined an arranged escape, arguing that having accepted the city's laws all his life he could not repudiate them when they went against him, and drank hemlock.

name: Battle of Leuctra
outcome: Decisive Theban victory

claims.text: Thebes defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC.
Epaminondas massed his left wing to unusual depth against the Spartan right.
Around 400 of 700 Spartiates present were killed.
Spartan power declined irreversibly after the battle.

summary: Epaminondas destroyed the myth of Spartan invincibility with a massed left wing, killing 400 of 700 Spartiates present.
body:
Convention put a general's best troops on the right, so the strongest wings of two armies never met. Epaminondas inverted it: he stacked his left wing fifty ranks deep against the Spartan right, held his own weaker right back at an angle, and attacked with the strong wing alone.

The Sacred Band led the charge. The Spartan right was broken before the rest of the line engaged. King Cleombrotus was killed, along with about 400 of the 700 Spartiates present.

Sparta had perhaps 1,500 full citizens left in total. Losing 400 in an afternoon was unrecoverable. Within a year Epaminondas invaded Laconia — which no enemy had done in living memory — and freed Messenia.

name: Accession of Philip II

claims.text: Philip II took power in Macedon in 359 BC after the death of Perdiccas III.
He restructured the Macedonian army around the sarissa phalanx.
Control of the Pangaeum mines gave Macedon substantial annual revenue.

summary: Philip took control of a Macedon that had just lost its king and 4,000 men, and began the reforms that would make it dominant.
body:
Perdiccas III was killed by the Illyrians with 4,000 Macedonians. Macedon faced simultaneous threats from Illyrians, Paeonians, Thracians and two rival claimants backed by Athens. Philip initially acted as guardian for the young Amyntas IV before taking the kingship himself, a transition whose precise constitutional form is obscured by later sources.

Philip bought off some enemies, defeated others, and rebuilt the army around the sarissa, deeper infantry formations and coordinated cavalry. He took Amphipolis and the Pangaeum gold mines, which gave him roughly 1,000 talents a year — more than Athens' entire imperial revenue at its height.

Within five years the immediate threats were gone. Within twenty-one, he controlled Greece.

name: Battle of Chaeronea
outcome: Decisive Macedonian victory

claims.text: Philip II defeated an allied Greek army at Chaeronea in 338 BC.
The Theban Sacred Band was destroyed in the battle.
A mass grave of 254 men lies beneath the Lion of Chaeronea.
Alexander commanded the cavalry on the Macedonian left.

summary: Philip II defeated the Athenian-Theban alliance in 338 BC, ending the independence of the Greek city-states.
body:
Around 30,000 Macedonians faced a similar number of allied Greeks. Philip commanded the right, Alexander at eighteen the left with the Companion cavalry.

Philip drew the Athenians forward with a controlled withdrawal — a manoeuvre only a professional army can execute — and as they advanced shouting that they would drive him to Macedon, the allied line stretched and a gap opened. Alexander charged into it.

The Sacred Band held their ground and were destroyed to a man. Philip treated Athens leniently, needing its fleet, and crushed Thebes. He then founded the League of Corinth with himself as *hegemon*, and announced a Panhellenic war against Persia.

name: The League of Corinth

claims.text: The League of Corinth was established in 337 BC with Philip II as hegemon.
Sparta refused to join.
The League authorised a joint campaign against Persia.
Macedonian garrisons were stationed at key Greek cities.

summary: Philip organised the Greek states into a federal league under his leadership, with a mandate to invade Persia.
body:
Formed in 337 BC, the League guaranteed members' constitutions, banned constitutional change by force, prohibited internal warfare, and elected Philip *hegemon* of a joint campaign against Persia. Sparta alone refused to join, and was left alone.

The legal form was a voluntary alliance of free states. The practical reality included Macedonian garrisons at Corinth, Thebes and Chalcis, and a ban on precisely the political changes that might threaten Macedonian influence.

It was the framework under which Alexander invaded Asia, and it gave the campaign the character of Panhellenic revenge for 480 BC rather than simple conquest.

name: Assassination of Philip II

claims.text: Philip II was assassinated at Aegae in 336 BC by his bodyguard Pausanias.
Pausanias was killed immediately while fleeing.
Ancient sources attribute a personal grievance as the motive.
Olympias or Alexander was involved in the plot.
Persia sponsored the assassination.

summary: Philip was murdered at his daughter's wedding in 336 BC by his bodyguard Pausanias, on the eve of the Persian invasion.
body:
The wedding at Aegae was a spectacle: Philip walked into the theatre without guards, deliberately, between statues of the twelve gods and a thirteenth of himself. Pausanias of Orestis, one of his own bodyguards, stabbed him and ran for horses waiting outside. He tripped and was killed on the spot.

The ancient explanation is personal: Pausanias had been assaulted by associates of Attalus and Philip had failed to give him justice. That the assassin was killed immediately, and that horses were waiting, has always invited suspicion of a wider plot.

Suspects proposed in antiquity and since include Olympias, sidelined by Philip's newest marriage; Alexander, whose succession was threatened by a potential heir of pure Macedonian blood; and Persia. There is no decisive evidence for any of them.

name: Battle of the Granicus
outcome: Macedonian victory

claims.text: Alexander defeated a Persian satrapal army at the Granicus in 334 BC.
His life was saved during the cavalry fighting by Cleitus.
Greek mercenaries in Persian service were massacred or enslaved after the battle.
He dedicated captured armour at Athens with an inscription excluding Sparta.

summary: Alexander's first victory in Asia, won by charging across a river against the Persian satrapal army.
body:
The Persian satraps drew up on the far bank of the Granicus with cavalry along the top and Greek mercenary infantry behind. Parmenion advised waiting for dawn. Alexander attacked immediately, leading the Companions across the river at an angle.

The fighting around him was desperate — a Persian axe split his helmet, and Cleitus the Black cut off the arm of the man about to finish him. Alexander would later kill Cleitus in a drunken quarrel.

After the cavalry broke, the Greek mercenaries were surrounded and massacred; the survivors were sent to forced labour in Macedon as traitors to the Panhellenic cause. Alexander sent 300 captured Persian panoplies to Athens, dedicated to Athena, with an inscription pointedly noting they came from "Alexander and the Greeks, except the Spartans".

name: Battle of Issus
outcome: Decisive Macedonian victory

claims.text: Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus in 333 BC.
The narrow terrain prevented the Persians from using their numerical advantage.
Darius' family was captured and treated with respect.
Darius offered substantial territorial concessions afterwards.

summary: Alexander defeated Darius III in person on a narrow coastal plain, capturing the Persian royal family.
body:
Darius manoeuvred behind Alexander and cut his supply lines — a good move that placed his own much larger army on a coastal strip too narrow to deploy in.

Alexander led the Companions in an oblique charge across the Pinarus river directly at Darius' chariot. The phalanx struggled crossing the riverbed against Greek mercenaries, but once Darius turned and fled the Persian line dissolved.

The royal camp fell with Darius' mother, wife and two daughters. Alexander guaranteed their status and treated them, the sources agree, with conspicuous respect. Darius offered ransom, territory west of the Euphrates and a daughter in marriage. Parmenion said he would accept if he were Alexander; Alexander replied that he would too, if he were Parmenion.

name: Siege of Tyre

claims.text: Alexander besieged Tyre for approximately seven months in 332 BC.
He constructed a causeway from the mainland to the island city.
The causeway permanently connected the island to the shore.
The population was massacred or enslaved after the city fell.

summary: Alexander took the island city of Tyre after seven months by building a causeway to it from the mainland.
body:
Tyre stood on an island 800 m offshore behind walls rising from the sea, and refused Alexander entry. He could not leave a Persian naval base behind him, so he built a mole out to the island — quarrying the abandoned mainland city for stone.

The Tyrians burned his siege towers with a fireship, dropped rocks to foul the approaches, and dropped heated sand on attackers, which got inside armour. Alexander eventually assembled a fleet from Sidon and Cyprus, blockaded both harbours, and mounted siege engines on lashed ships.

When the wall was breached the city was sacked: sources report 8,000 killed and 30,000 sold into slavery. The mole silted up and permanently joined Tyre to the mainland — a geographic change still visible on any map.

name: Founding of Alexandria

claims.text: Alexander founded Alexandria in Egypt in 331 BC.
The site provided a double harbour and access to inland waterways.
Alexander visited the oracle of Ammon at Siwa.
He was greeted at Siwa as the son of the god.

summary: Alexander laid out a new city on the Egyptian coast that became the intellectual capital of the ancient world.
body:
Alexander chose a site on a limestone ridge between the sea and Lake Mareotis, with the island of Pharos providing a natural double harbour and freshwater access inland. It was an outstanding choice of site, and the city has been continuously important for 2,300 years.

The story goes that, lacking chalk, the surveyors marked the street plan with barley meal, and birds descended and ate it — read by the seers as a sign that the city would feed the world.

Alexander also travelled to the oracle of Ammon at Siwa, deep in the desert, and was reportedly greeted as son of the god. What he asked and was told, he never disclosed.

name: Battle of Gaugamela
outcome: Decisive Macedonian victory; Persian empire collapses

claims.text: Alexander defeated Darius III at Gaugamela on 1 October 331 BC.
A Babylonian astronomical record fixes the date precisely.
Darius had the battlefield levelled in advance for chariots.
Alexander broke off pursuit to relieve Parmenion on the left.

summary: Alexander destroyed the main Persian army on 1 October 331 BC, effectively ending the Achaemenid Empire.
body:
Darius chose a wide plain and levelled it so his scythed chariots and cavalry could operate, and assembled contingents from across the empire including Bactrians, Scythians and fifteen elephants.

Alexander advanced obliquely to the right, forcing the Persian left to extend to prevent an outflanking. When that stretching opened a gap, he wheeled the Companions into a wedge aimed directly at Darius.

Darius fled again. On the Macedonian left Parmenion was nearly overwhelmed and Persian raiders reached the baggage camp; Alexander had to abandon the pursuit to help. The empire, however, was finished — Babylon and Susa surrendered without a fight.

A Babylonian astronomical diary records a lunar eclipse eleven days earlier, fixing the date to 1 October 331 BC.

name: The burning of Persepolis

claims.text: The palace complex at Persepolis was destroyed by fire in 330 BC.
Alexander captured an enormous treasury at Persepolis.
The fire preserved administrative tablets by baking them.
The burning was deliberate policy rather than a drunken act.

summary: Alexander burned the Achaemenid ceremonial capital in 330 BC — whether as policy or on a drunken impulse is disputed.
body:
Alexander took Persepolis in early 330 BC and its treasury, reportedly 120,000 talents, more than any state in the Greek world had ever held.

Months later the palace complex burned. Arrian, following Ptolemy, presents it as a deliberate act of vengeance for Xerxes' burning of Athens, and records Parmenion arguing against destroying what was now Alexander's own property. Diodorus, Curtius and Plutarch describe a drunken feast at which the Athenian courtesan Thais urged that a woman's hand should avenge the Acropolis, and Alexander threw the first torch.

Excavation confirms an intense fire — burnt cedar beams, ash layers, melted metal. It cannot say why. The fire also baked the administrative tablets in the fortification walls, preserving them.

name: Battle of the Hydaspes
outcome: Macedonian victory; Porus reinstated as satrap

claims.text: Alexander defeated Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BC.
Porus deployed a large force of war elephants.
Alexander crossed the river upstream under cover of a storm.
Bucephalus died at or shortly after the battle.
It was the costliest battle of Alexander's career.

summary: Alexander's hardest-fought victory, against Porus and his war elephants in monsoon rain on the Jhelum river.
body:
The river was swollen by monsoon and Porus held the far bank with around 200 elephants — which horses will not approach. Alexander spent weeks making noisy night movements until the Indians stopped responding, then crossed 27 km upstream in a storm.

The battle was brutal. The phalanx opened lanes to let elephants pass through rather than break, and attacked their handlers and trunks; wounded and panicking elephants trampled troops on both sides. Alexander used his cavalry on one flank to draw the Indian horse away, then took them in the rear with a second detachment.

Bucephalus, his horse for twenty years, died after the battle, and Alexander founded a city named for him. It was his last great battle: at the Hyphasis shortly afterwards, his army refused to go further east.

name: Death of Alexander

claims.text: Alexander died at Babylon in June 323 BC after an illness of about eleven days.
Babylonian astronomical diaries independently record the death.
He left no adult heir capable of holding the empire together.
He was poisoned.
The "to the strongest" succession remark was actually made.

summary: Alexander died at Babylon in June 323 BC aged 32, leaving no viable heir and an empire that fragmented immediately.
body:
He fell ill after a prolonged banquet and declined over eleven days with fever, becoming unable to speak. Soldiers filed past his bed; he could only move his eyes. He died on 10 or 11 June 323 BC.

His wife Roxana was pregnant; his half-brother Arrhidaeus had a cognitive disability. Asked who should succeed, he reportedly said "to the strongest" — which is what happened, over forty years of wars among his generals. Both his son and his half-brother were eventually murdered.

Causes proposed include malaria, typhoid, acute pancreatitis, West Nile virus, complications from the untreated lung wound he took in India, and poison. Plutarch, writing four centuries later, notes that no suspicion of poison arose at the time. The Babylonian astronomical diaries record the king's death independently, confirming the date.

name: Wars of the Diadochi
outcome: Empire divided into Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Antigonid kingdoms

claims.text: Alexander's generals fought for control of the empire from 322 to 281 BC.
The successors assumed royal titles from 306 BC.
Alexander's surviving family members were killed during the conflicts.
The wars produced three principal successor kingdoms.

summary: Forty years of war among Alexander's generals that carved the empire into the Hellenistic kingdoms.
body:
The generals first claimed to govern for Alexander's heirs, then stopped pretending. From 306 BC they took royal titles outright.

The wars were fought on an enormous scale — Ipsus in 301 BC involved perhaps 150,000 men and 475 elephants — and were settled by the near-total elimination of Alexander's family. Roxana and her son Alexander IV, Arrhidaeus, Olympias, and Alexander's sister Cleopatra were all killed.

By 281 BC the map was set: Ptolemies in Egypt, Seleucids across Asia, Antigonids in Macedon, with Pergamon and Bactria emerging later. This division held, roughly, until Rome dismantled it.

name: Battle of Ipsus
outcome: Antigonus killed; unified empire permanently ended

claims.text: Antigonus I was defeated and killed at Ipsus in 301 BC.
Seleucus deployed around 400 war elephants obtained from India.
The elephants prevented Demetrius' cavalry from rejoining the battle.
The battle ended prospects of reuniting Alexander's empire.

summary: The largest battle of the Diadochi wars, where Seleucus' 400 elephants decided the fate of Alexander's empire.
body:
Antigonus the One-Eyed came closest to reuniting Alexander's empire, which is why the others allied against him. At Ipsus in Phrygia perhaps 150,000 men met.

Demetrius drove off the opposing cavalry and pursued too far. Seleucus then interposed his 400 war elephants — obtained from Chandragupta Maurya in exchange for eastern territory — as a screen between Demetrius and the battlefield. Horses will not approach elephants, and Demetrius could not get back.

Antigonus, aged around 80, was left unsupported and killed by javelins, reportedly still expecting his son to return. With him died the last realistic prospect of a single empire.

name: Battle of Salamis (Cyprus)
outcome: Decisive Antigonid naval victory; triggered royal titles across the Successor states

claims.text: Demetrius Poliorcetes defeated a Ptolemaic fleet off Salamis in 306 BC and took control of Cyprus.
Ptolemy's relief fleet numbered roughly 140 ships.
News of the victory led Antigonus I and Demetrius to proclaim themselves kings, and the other Successors followed within about a year.
The battle is treated as marking the start of open, independent Hellenistic kingship.

summary: Demetrius Poliorcetes destroyed a Ptolemaic fleet off Cyprus — a victory that pushed the Successors to start calling themselves kings.
body:
Demetrius landed on Cyprus, defeated Ptolemy's brother Menelaus at sea, and besieged Salamis. Ptolemy sailed to relieve it with a fleet of roughly 140 ships. Demetrius met him in the open water outside the harbour rather than let him land reinforcements, and won overwhelmingly — accounts report most of the Ptolemaic fleet sunk or captured and thousands of soldiers taken prisoner. Ptolemy escaped to Egypt; Menelaus surrendered the city and the island.

Within weeks of the news reaching him, Antigonus I had himself and Demetrius proclaimed *basileus* — king — the first of Alexander's former generals to do so outright rather than govern as regents for his heirs, all of whom were by then dead. Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander followed within about a year. The pretence of a single Argead empire ended there; what followed were openly rival Hellenistic kingdoms.

name: Founding of the Library of Alexandria

claims.text: The Ptolemies founded a Museum and Library at Alexandria in the early 3rd century BC.
Resident scholars were salaried and housed by the state.
Alexandrian scholars produced critical editions of Homer and invented textual sigla.
Callimachus produced a catalogue of the collection.
The Library was destroyed in a single catastrophic event.

summary: The Ptolemies founded a Museum and Library that salaried scholars and attempted to collect every book in the world.
body:
The Museum was a research institution: resident scholars received a salary, meals, lodging and exemption from taxes, and were expected only to work. It is the earliest state-funded research institute known.

Acquisition was aggressive. Ships entering the harbour were searched for books, which were copied — with the copies returned and the originals kept. Ptolemy III borrowed the official Athenian texts of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides against an enormous deposit, had them copied, kept the originals and forfeited the money.

The scholarship was serious: Zenodotus and Aristarchus produced critical editions of Homer and invented the textual apparatus — obelus and asterisk — still used today. Callimachus catalogued the collection in 120 volumes, effectively founding library science.

The Library declined gradually through fire, funding cuts and the expulsion of scholars, rather than in one dramatic destruction.

name: Eratosthenes measures the Earth

claims.text: Eratosthenes estimated the Earth's circumference from shadow angles at two locations.
Greek astronomers already accepted that the Earth is spherical.
His result was accurate to within a few percent of the true value.

summary: Using shadow angles at two Egyptian cities, Eratosthenes calculated the Earth's circumference to within a few percent.
body:
The method requires only a stick, a well and a measured distance. At Syene the sun was directly overhead at noon on the summer solstice — no shadow in a deep well. At Alexandria, roughly due north, a vertical gnomon cast a shadow of about 7.2° at the same moment.

If the Earth is a sphere and the sun's rays are effectively parallel, that 7.2° is 1/50th of a full circle, so the distance between the cities is 1/50th of the circumference. Multiplying by 50 gave about 250,000 stades.

How accurate this is depends on the length of his stade, which is not certain. On the most probable value the error is under 2%. That the Earth is spherical was already standard among educated Greeks — Aristotle had argued it from the shape of the shadow during lunar eclipses. Eratosthenes measured it.

name: Battle of Cynoscephalae
outcome: Roman victory; Macedonian hegemony over Greece ends

claims.text: Rome defeated Philip V at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC.
Part of the Macedonian army was caught before completing its deployment.
A flanking movement by Roman maniples attacked the phalanx from the rear.
Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks at the Isthmian Games in 196 BC.

summary: The Roman legion defeated the Macedonian phalanx for the first time, on broken ground in Thessaly.
body:
The two armies collided unexpectedly in fog on the "Dog's Heads" ridge. Philip's right formed up and pushed the Roman left back downhill. His left, still in march column on rough ground, was caught before it could deploy.

An unnamed Roman tribune then took twenty maniples out of the victorious Roman right and marched them into the rear of Philip's successful wing. A phalanx cannot turn. It was destroyed from behind.

Polybius drew the conclusion that became doctrine: the phalanx is unbeatable frontally on level ground and helpless if it cannot get that ground or maintain its line. Flamininus then proclaimed at the Isthmian Games that the Greek cities were free — to enormous acclaim, and under Roman supervision.

name: Battle of Pydna
outcome: Decisive Roman victory; Macedonian monarchy abolished

claims.text: Rome destroyed the Macedonian army at Pydna in 168 BC.
The Macedonian kingdom was abolished after the battle.
Roman maniples exploited gaps opening in the phalanx on uneven ground.
Perseus was captured and displayed in a Roman triumph.

summary: Rome destroyed the Macedonian army in under an hour, abolishing the kingdom of Alexander's successors.
body:
The phalanx advanced and initially drove the legions back — Aemilius Paullus later said the sight of that pike wall coming on was the most frightening thing he had ever seen.

But the ground was uneven, and as the phalanx pushed forward its line lost continuity. Paullus ordered his maniples into the gaps. Once inside the pike points, legionaries with the *gladius* were fighting men holding a six-metre pole in both hands who could not turn or draw.

The battle lasted about an hour. Perseus fled and was captured, and paraded in Paullus' triumph. The Macedonian kingdom was abolished and divided into four republics; two decades later it became a province.

name: The sack of Corinth

claims.text: Rome destroyed Corinth in 146 BC after defeating the Achaean League.
The population was killed or enslaved and the city's art looted.
Carthage was destroyed by Rome in the same year.
Corinth was refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BC.

summary: Rome destroyed Corinth in 146 BC, killing or enslaving its population as a warning to the rest of Greece.
body:
The Achaean League, provoked by Roman demands that it dismantle itself, went to war and lost quickly. Lucius Mummius took Corinth, killed the men, sold the women and children into slavery, looted the art and burned the city.

It was policy. Rome destroyed Carthage the same year. The message to the Greek world was that resistance would not be punished proportionally.

Polybius, a Greek who had spent seventeen years in Rome, arrived afterwards and had the unenviable task of helping organise the settlement of his own conquered homeland. He records Mummius' famous ignorance about the art he was shipping — warning the contractors that if they lost any of it they would have to replace it.

Corinth lay largely empty until Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC.

name: Sulla sacks Athens

claims.text: Sulla besieged and stormed Athens in 86 BC.
A destruction layer of this date is identifiable in the Athenian Agora.
Sulla felled the groves of the Academy and Lyceum for siege material.
Aristotle's library was taken to Rome as part of the plunder.

summary: Sulla stormed Athens in 86 BC after it sided with Mithridates, causing damage the city never fully recovered from.
body:
Athens joined Mithridates of Pontus against Rome, having suffered under Roman tax farmers. Sulla besieged the city through the winter, and the population starved — sources report people eating boiled shoe leather.

He stormed it on 1 March 86 BC. The killing in the Kerameikos was severe enough that Plutarch reports blood running through the gate. Sulla stopped the massacre, saying he spared the many for the sake of the few — a reference to Athens' past rather than its present.

He cut the sacred groves of the Academy and the Lyceum for siege timber, looted extensively, and shipped Aristotle's library to Rome. Archaeologically the destruction layer is clear across the Agora. Athens remained a revered university town but was never again politically significant.

name: Battle of Actium
outcome: Decisive victory for Octavian

claims.text: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium on 2 September 31 BC.
Cleopatra's squadron left the battle and Antony followed.
Antony's land army surrendered within days.
The withdrawal was a planned breakout rather than a betrayal.

summary: Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra on 2 September 31 BC, effectively ending the Hellenistic age.
body:
Antony and Cleopatra were blockaded in the Ambracian Gulf with a fleet weakened by malaria and desertion; Antony had already burned ships he could not crew.

He attempted a breakout. Mid-battle Cleopatra's squadron of sixty ships raised sail and ran south. Antony transferred to a lighter ship and followed, leaving his fleet and his army — which surrendered a week later.

Octavian's version, which became the official one, framed this as a foreign queen's betrayal and a Roman general's enslavement to her. A more sober reading is that the treasury and the escape were the objective and the fighting was cover. Either way, within a year both were dead and Egypt was Roman.

name: Death of Cleopatra and annexation of Egypt

claims.text: Cleopatra VII died in Alexandria in August 30 BC.
Egypt was annexed by Rome as an imperial possession in 30 BC.
Her son Caesarion was executed.
She died from a snake bite.

summary: Cleopatra VII died in August 30 BC; Egypt became a Roman province, ending the last Hellenistic kingdom.
body:
Antony killed himself on a false report of her death. Cleopatra was captured, and negotiated — or appeared to — while learning that Octavian intended to display her in his triumph. She died shortly after, with her attendants Iras and Charmion.

Plutarch reports the asp smuggled in a basket of figs, and immediately concedes that nobody knows the truth: some said poison hidden in a hollow comb, and the two small marks on her arm were the only evidence. A snake was never found.

Octavian annexed Egypt not as a normal province but as his personal possession, governed by a prefect, with senators forbidden to enter without permission — Egyptian grain fed Rome, and he was not going to let a rival control it. Caesarion, her son by Caesar, was killed. The Ptolemaic dynasty, founded 293 years earlier, ended.

name: Decipherment of Linear B

claims.text: Ventris deciphered Linear B in 1952, identifying the language as Greek.
Cretan place names provided the initial breakthrough.
Tablet PY Ta 641 provided independent confirmation.
The decipherment extended attested Greek back roughly five centuries.

summary: Michael Ventris showed in 1952 that Linear B recorded Greek, opening five centuries of previously mute history.
body:
Ventris built a grid organising the syllabic signs by shared consonant and vowel without assuming any sound values, working purely from distributional patterns in the texts.

He noticed sign-groups appearing only on Knossos tablets, likely place names, and tested Cretan toponyms against them. Amnisos, Knossos and Tulissos produced consistent values that then worked across other words.

The resulting language was Greek — an archaic form, but unmistakably Greek. Ventris had expected something related to Etruscan and initially assumed he had made an error. He announced it on BBC radio in June 1952. John Chadwick joined him, and Carl Blegen's Pylos tablet PY Ta 641, where the values produced *ti-ri-po-de* beside pictures of tripods, provided independent confirmation.

The result pushed attested Greek back 500 years before Homer and made the Mycenaean world historical rather than merely archaeological.

name: The Greco-Persian Wars
combatants: Greek city-states (led by Athens and Sparta)
outcome: Greek victory; Persia withdraws from the Aegean and mainland Greece

claims.text: The wars began with the Ionian Revolt in 499 BC and included two full-scale Persian invasions of mainland Greece, in 490 and 480–479 BC.
The war is traditionally held to have ended with the Peace of Callias in 449 BC, in which Persia accepted Greek autonomy in Ionia.
The Delian League, formed in 478 BC as a continuing anti-Persian alliance, grew directly out of the war's aftermath.
Herodotus' Histories, the main surviving narrative source, was written a generation after the events it describes.

summary: Two Persian invasions of Greece, repelled at Marathon and then at Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea, that reshaped the Aegean world for a century.
body:
The wars opened with the Ionian Revolt of 499–494 BC, a failed uprising by Greek cities on the Anatolian coast against Persian rule, in which Athens' brief involvement gave Darius I a pretext for direct action against the mainland. His 490 BC expedition was stopped at Marathon; a decade later his son Xerxes returned with a vastly larger force, winning at Thermopylae and burning Athens before losing the fleet at Salamis and, the following year, the army at Plataea, with the simultaneous naval victory at Mycale finishing Persian sea power in the Aegean.

Fighting continued at a lower intensity for another generation. Athens and its allies formed the Delian League in 478 BC explicitly to keep fighting Persia and liberate remaining Greek cities under its rule, winning a further major victory under Cimon at the Eurymedon river around 466 BC. Ancient tradition holds that the conflict was formally ended by the Peace of Callias in 449 BC, in which Persia recognised the autonomy of the Ionian Greek cities — though the treaty's existence and exact terms are disputed by modern historians, since no Greek source before the fourth century mentions it directly.

The war's most lasting consequence was institutional rather than territorial: the alliance built to fight Persia did not disband once Persia was contained, and within a generation had become the Athenian empire.

name: The Macedonian Wars
outcome: Macedon annexed as a Roman province

claims.text: Rome and Macedon fought four separate wars between 214 and 148 BC.
The Second Macedonian War ended with Flamininus's victory over Philip V at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC.
The Third Macedonian War ended with Aemilius Paullus's victory over Perseus at Pydna in 168 BC, after which the monarchy was abolished.
The Fourth Macedonian War, against the pretender Andriscus, ended with Macedon's direct annexation as a Roman province in 148 BC.

summary: Four wars over seven decades in which Rome dismantled the kingdom Philip II and Alexander had built, ending in direct provincial rule.
body:
The first war (214–205 BC), fought while Rome was still consumed by Hannibal in Italy, was a minor sideshow that changed little. The second (200–196 BC) was decisive: Flamininus defeated Philip V at Cynoscephalae and then proclaimed the freedom of the Greek cities at the Isthmian Games, ending Macedonian hegemony over Greece while leaving the kingdom itself intact under Roman oversight.

Philip's son Perseus inherited a weakened but still functioning state, and renewed war with Rome broke out in 171 BC. Aemilius Paullus destroyed the Macedonian army at Pydna in 168 BC in under an hour; Perseus was captured, and the monarchy — the same royal house, in unbroken line, that had produced Philip II and Alexander — was abolished outright. Macedon was split into four notionally independent republics under Roman supervision.

That arrangement lasted twenty years. When a pretender named Andriscus, claiming descent from Perseus, briefly restored the monarchy and defeated a Roman army, Rome answered with direct annexation: Macedon became a Roman province in 148 BC, ending both the war and any prospect of Macedonian independence. The Achaean War of 146 BC, which brought the destruction of Corinth, followed within two years as Rome extended the same settlement across the rest of mainland Greece.

name: Battle of Mycale
outcome: Decisive Greek victory; Persian naval power in the Aegean destroyed

claims.text: A Greek fleet under the Spartan king Leotychidas and the Athenian Xanthippus destroyed the beached Persian fleet at Cape Mycale in 479 BC.
Ancient tradition holds the battle took place on the same day as Plataea.
Ionian Greek cities revolted from Persian rule in the battle's aftermath.

summary: A Greek fleet destroyed the beached Persian navy at Mycale in 479 BC, on the same day tradition places the victory at Plataea, ending Persian sea power in the Aegean.
body:
After Salamis, the remaining Persian fleet had drawn up on the beach at Mycale, opposite Samos, under the protection of a land garrison, judging open battle at sea against the Greeks too risky. The Greek fleet, initially reluctant, was persuaded by Samian envoys and Ionian Greek exiles to cross and attack anyway.

The Greeks landed and stormed the fortified camp; the Persian force, largely composed of demoralised Ionian Greek conscripts who reportedly withdrew from the fighting or actively turned on their Persian officers once the issue was in doubt, collapsed. Herodotus places the battle on the very day of Plataea, a coincidence many modern historians treat as a literary flourish rather than fact, though the two victories certainly fell close together.

Its immediate consequence was an open revolt of the Ionian Greek cities from Persian rule, which the newly formed Delian League was built specifically to protect and extend — Mycale marks the point where the defensive war became a war of liberation.

name: Battle of the Eurymedon
outcome: Decisive Delian League victory, at sea and on land in a single day

claims.text: Cimon led a Delian League fleet to victory over a Persian fleet at the mouth of the Eurymedon river, then landed and defeated Persian land forces the same day.
Around 200 Phoenician ships in Persian service were captured or destroyed.
The victory effectively ended major Persian naval activity in the Aegean for a generation.

summary: Cimon destroyed a Persian fleet and then its supporting army on the same day at the mouth of the Eurymedon, around 466 BC.
body:
Cimon caught the Persian fleet at anchor off the Pamphylian coast and destroyed or captured it before it could properly deploy, then, learning that Persian reinforcements had landed troops nearby, landed his own marines the same day and routed them too — an unusual double victory that ancient writers treated as an exceptional feat even by Athenian standards.

The scale of the win, whatever the exact numbers Plutarch and other later sources report, removed Persia as an active naval threat in the Aegean for a generation, letting the Delian League's members refocus its enormous common treasury toward Athens' own ends rather than continuous campaigning. The spoils are traditionally linked to a wave of Athenian public building in the years that followed, foreshadowing the far larger building program Pericles would launch after the mid-century peace with Persia.

name: Battle of Sphacteria
outcome: Athenian victory; Spartan hoplites surrender

claims.text: Athenian forces under Demosthenes and Cleon trapped and forced the surrender of a Spartan garrison on the island of Sphacteria in 425 BC.
Around 120 of the surrendering troops were full Spartan citizens (Spartiates), a small fraction of the total Spartan citizen body.
It was the first time Spartan hoplites had surrendered in battle rather than fighting to the death.
The captured Spartiates were held hostage at Athens and constrained Spartan strategy for years afterward.

summary: An Athenian force trapped a Spartan garrison on Sphacteria in 425 BC and forced roughly 120 Spartan citizens to surrender — an unprecedented shock to Sparta's military prestige.
body:
A chance Athenian landing at Pylos, on the Spartan mainland's own coast, left a Spartan force stranded on the offshore island of Sphacteria when the Athenian fleet cut off their escape. The siege dragged on until Cleon, an Athenian politician with no military reputation who had rashly promised the assembly a quick result, was sent out with the general Demosthenes and, against most expectations, actually delivered one: the Spartan position was stormed and the survivors surrendered.

The surrender itself was the real shock. Spartan citizen-soldiers were expected to die rather than yield, and the roughly 120 Spartiates taken prisoner represented a significant fraction of Sparta's entire full-citizen fighting body — Sparta's citizen population was already in long-term decline, and it could not afford this loss lightly. Held hostage at Athens, the prisoners gave Athens real leverage: Sparta avoided invading Attica for years afterward for fear of what might happen to them.

Thucydides frames the episode partly as an argument about Athenian democratic politics — Cleon's success was resented as much as celebrated, since it vindicated a demagogue's gamble over the caution of more established leaders.

name: Battle of Delium
outcome: Decisive Boeotian victory; Athenian invasion of Boeotia repelled

claims.text: A Boeotian army led by Thebes defeated an invading Athenian force at Delium in 424 BC.
Socrates served as a hoplite in the battle and was noted for his composure during the retreat.
The Theban contingent's unusually deep phalanx formation contributed to the victory.

summary: Thebes led a Boeotian army to a decisive victory over an invading Athenian force at Delium in 424 BC, in which Socrates served and reportedly distinguished himself in the retreat.
body:
Athens attempted to knock Boeotia, Thebes' regional league, out of the war by seizing and fortifying the sanctuary of Delium as a forward base. A Boeotian army caught the Athenian force as it withdrew, and won decisively — one of the largest hoplite battles of the war's first phase and a serious check on Athenian ambitions on land.
