Among the Athenian hoplites that day was Socrates, then in his mid-forties; Plato and other later sources describe him as remaining calm and orderly during the rout, a detail later writers used to illustrate the same self-possession he showed throughout his life, on the battlefield as much as in the agora.

The Theban infantry's notably deep formation at Delium is sometimes read by modern historians as an early ancestor of the much deeper, more radical phalanx Epaminondas would use to break Sparta at Leuctra half a century later — a continuous Theban tactical tradition of concentrating force on one flank rather than spreading it evenly along the line.

name: Battle of Mantinea (418 BC)
outcome: Decisive Spartan victory; Spartan military prestige restored

claims.text: A Spartan-led army defeated a coalition of Argos, Athens and Mantinea at Mantinea in 418 BC.
Thucydides describes it as the largest battle fought among Greek states in a very long time.
The victory restored Spartan military confidence after the humiliation of Sphacteria.

summary: Sparta defeated a coalition led by Argos and Athens at Mantinea in 418 BC, restoring its military reputation after the surrender at Sphacteria.
body:
The years after the Peace of Nicias (421 BC) were an uneasy, incomplete truce rather than real peace, and Argos assembled a coalition with Athens and Mantinea to challenge Spartan dominance of the Peloponnese while Sparta still seemed weakened by Sphacteria. The armies met at Mantinea in what Thucydides calls the largest gathering of Greek hoplites in a great many years.

Sparta's disciplined manoeuvring under King Agis II won the day, in the last major set-piece hoplite battle of the war's central phase. The defeat broke up the anti-Spartan coalition and restored confidence in Spartan arms after the shock of Sphacteria three years earlier — a psychological recovery at least as significant as the battle's immediate territorial consequences, which were modest.

name: Battle of Mantinea (362 BC)
outcome: Theban tactical victory; Epaminondas killed, Theban hegemony collapses

claims.text: Epaminondas led a Boeotian army to tactical victory over a Spartan-Athenian coalition at Mantinea in 362 BC, using the same massed-wing tactic as at Leuctra.
Epaminondas was killed at the moment of victory.
Xenophon's Hellenica ends its narrative with this battle, describing the confusion that followed as greater than before it.
Theban hegemony over Greece collapsed within a few years of Epaminondas's death.

summary: Epaminondas won again at Mantinea in 362 BC using the tactics that had broken Sparta at Leuctra — and died in the moment of victory, taking Theban hegemony down with him.
body:
Nine years after Leuctra, Epaminondas faced a coalition of Sparta, Athens and others determined to check continued Theban dominance of Greece. He repeated the tactic that had won at Leuctra, massing an unusually deep strike force on one wing while holding the rest of the line back, and broke the opposing formation just as decisively.

He was struck down, probably by a spear, at the height of the breakthrough. Ancient accounts describe him asking, as he lay dying, whether his shield was safe and whether the Thebans had won, and being satisfied enough by the answers to allow himself to die — a story polished by later tradition into something close to a set-piece, whether or not every detail is literal.

Xenophon's Hellenica, the main narrative source for the period, ends its account precisely here, closing with the observation that the battle left Greece in greater confusion and uncertainty than before it had been fought — a fitting epitaph for a war that changed hegemony without settling anything. Without Epaminondas, Thebes had no comparable leader, and its brief dominance of Greek affairs collapsed within a few years, leaving no power strong enough to resist the rise of Macedon under Philip II a generation later.

name: Battle of Arginusae
outcome: Athenian victory; aftermath triggers a domestic political crisis

claims.text: An Athenian fleet defeated a Spartan fleet near the Arginusae islands in 406 BC.
A storm afterward prevented the recovery of shipwrecked Athenian sailors and the dead.
The victorious generals were tried collectively and executed at Athens for the failure to rescue survivors, in a process later writers considered illegal.
Socrates, serving that year as a member of the presiding council, refused to allow the illegal collective vote to proceed.

summary: Athens won its last major naval victory of the war at Arginusae in 406 BC, then executed the victorious generals in a legally dubious mass trial over the storm-hampered rescue that followed.
body:
Facing a Spartan fleet with Athens' own survival at stake, an emergency Athenian force — including newly freed slaves rowing alongside citizens — won a clear victory near the Arginusae islands, off the Anatolian coast. It should have been an unqualified triumph, arguably the last real chance to recover from the war's long decline.

A storm broke immediately afterward, preventing the generals from recovering the crews of disabled ships and the bodies of the dead — a failure that was, in the circumstances, arguably unavoidable, but which the Athenian assembly treated as a capital offence. In a legally irregular move, the assembly voted to try all the generals together rather than individually as the law required; Socrates, serving that year on the presiding council (prytany), was the sole member to refuse to put the illegal motion to a vote, at real personal risk. He was overruled, and six generals were executed.

Xenophon's account presents the episode as a moment of collective madness the Athenians came to regret almost immediately afterward — and a self-inflicted wound the city, already short of experienced commanders, could not really afford so close to its final defeat.

name: Battle of Corupedium
outcome: Decisive Seleucid victory; Lysimachus killed

claims.text: Seleucus I defeated and killed Lysimachus at Corupedium in Lydia in 281 BC.
Lysimachus was the last of Alexander's original companions and successors still living at the time of the battle.
Seleucus was assassinated within months of the victory, before he could unify the territory he had just won.

summary: Seleucus killed his old comrade-in-arms Lysimachus at Corupedium in 281 BC, ending the last rivalry among Alexander's original successors.
body:
Lysimachus and Seleucus had fought on the same side at Ipsus twenty years earlier, but rivalry over Asia Minor and a poisonous family dispute inside Lysimachus's own court — his execution of his son Agathocles on the accusation of his wife Arsinoe had driven many of his own supporters toward Seleucus — brought the two old men to battle at Corupedium in Lydia.

Seleucus won decisively, and Lysimachus was killed in the fighting — the last of Alexander's original bodyguards and generals to die, some four decades after Alexander himself. For a brief moment, Seleucus stood as the sole survivor of that generation, master of nearly the whole of Alexander's former empire outside Egypt.

It did not last. Crossing into Europe to claim Macedon itself — the one part of Alexander's inheritance he had never held — Seleucus was assassinated within months by Ptolemy Keraunos, a disaffected son of Ptolemy I. His own son Antiochus I inherited the Seleucid heartland, while Macedon passed through a chaotic decade before settling, eventually, on Antigonus I's grandson — closing the wars of the Diadochi with the three-kingdom map that defined the Hellenistic world.

name: Siege of Rhodes
outcome: Rhodian victory; siege abandoned by negotiated settlement

claims.text: Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged Rhodes for about a year, 305–304 BC, after it refused to join Antigonid campaigns against Ptolemy.
He deployed exceptionally large siege engines, including the "Helepolis" siege tower.
Rhodes held out and negotiated a settlement preserving its independence.
The Rhodians funded the Colossus of Rhodes partly from the sale of equipment Demetrius abandoned.

summary: Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged Rhodes for a year with the largest siege engines the Greek world had seen, and failed to take it.
body:
Rhodes had stayed on good terms with Ptolemy of Egypt, its main trading partner, and refused Antigonus's demand to join the war against him. Demetrius arrived to force the issue with a fleet and army built around siege technology on an unprecedented scale, above all the Helepolis — an armoured, multi-storey siege tower reportedly requiring thousands of men to move, packed with catapults and ballistae.

Rhodes withstood a year of assault, sabotaging engines, holding key defensive points and receiving occasional relief supplies past the blockade. Neither side could force a decision, and a negotiated peace left Rhodes formally independent while acknowledging a friendly relationship with Antigonus — a result close enough to victory for the Rhodians that they kept celebrating it for centuries.

Tradition holds that the Rhodians sold the siege equipment Demetrius left behind and used the proceeds toward a colossal bronze statue of their patron god Helios, standing some 30 metres tall near the harbour — the Colossus of Rhodes, later counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and toppled by an earthquake less than a century after it was raised.

name: Battle of Magnesia
outcome: Decisive Roman victory; Seleucid power in Anatolia ended

claims.text: A Roman-led army defeated Antiochus III's Seleucid army at Magnesia ad Sipylum in 190 BC.
The Roman general Lucius Cornelius Scipio was accompanied by his brother, Scipio Africanus, acting as a legate.
The following Treaty of Apamea (188 BC) forced the Seleucids to withdraw from Anatolia north and west of the Taurus mountains.
The kingdom of Pergamon and Rhodes gained substantial territory from the settlement.

summary: Rome broke Antiochus III's Seleucid army at Magnesia in 190 BC, ending Seleucid power west of the Taurus mountains for good.
body:
Antiochus III, fresh from campaigns that had earned him the title "the Great" by restoring much of the Seleucid Empire's eastern territory, overreached by intervening in Greece and clashing directly with Rome. Driven out of Greece itself at Thermopylae in 191 BC, he assembled a large army — including scythed chariots and war elephants — to meet the Romans in Anatolia the following year.

At Magnesia, Roman legions and their Pergamene allies broke the Seleucid line despite being significantly outnumbered; the elephants and chariots, meant to overawe the Romans, reportedly caused as much disruption to their own side as to the enemy once panicked. The Roman commander, Lucius Cornelius Scipio, campaigned with his more famous brother Scipio Africanus, the victor over Hannibal, serving alongside him as a legate — a detail ancient sources treat as adding extra weight to the victory.

The Treaty of Apamea that followed in 188 BC was one of the most consequential settlements of the Hellenistic period: it stripped the Seleucid Empire of all territory in Anatolia north and west of the Taurus mountains, handing most of it to Rome's allies Pergamon and Rhodes, and imposed a crippling war indemnity. The Seleucid Empire never again threatened the Aegean world directly, and Rome's role as the ultimate arbiter of Hellenistic affairs was now unmistakable.
